articles.text: The Piedmont Scouting community gathered at Piedmont Community Church’s Guild Hall on Thursday, April 18 for Piedmont Scout Council’s 103rd annual Awards Dinner and Recognition ceremony. The event has been held every year since the council was officially chartered with the national organization in 1921 and recognizes outstanding service by local scouts and volunteers. In addition to the many awards and recognitions received that night, Lisa Gros, a longtime leader of Troop 6 at Corpus Christi Catholic Church and a former President of the Piedmont Council Executive Board, was presented with the highest award for adult volunteers, the Silver Beaver Award. The event began with drinks and light appetizers served in the church’s courtyard. Paul Jahn presented the President’s Award to former Eagle Scout Tom Smegal III for his continued contributions to Piedmont scouting as Chair of the annual Christmas Tree Lot. “Let’s be honest. These public meetings will result in the adoption of a new city budget by the City Council on Monday, June 17. Members of the public are encouraged to attend and provide feedback. All other meetings will be held in City Hall. The proposed budget is expected to be published for review and feedback in early May. In previous years, public budget discussions began in May, following the release of the proposed budget. The earlier start this year indicates the City’s move towards longer-term planning, a shift that has been underway for several years at the recommendation of the City’s Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee. It countenances violence. It depicts God commanding violence. Further, Joshua describes one group of people taking the land of another. In human history, including the history that is unfolding even now, such narratives have given rise to tragedies of epic proportion. articles.text: Piedmont’s annual Arbor Day celebration will be held this Friday, April 26, from 3 to 5 p.m. outside the Community Hall. In addition to the announcement of this year’s heritage tree selections by the Park Commission, the event will also include a meet-and-greet event with a raptor hosted by the Lindsay Wildlife Center. In front of Community Hall, the city will display some of its trucks and bulldozers to give the public a better idea of its role in maintaining local flora. Arts and crafts activities for kids will also be available. The City’s Arbor Day event, which began in 2007, celebrates the nearly 9,000 trees maintained by the Public Works Department in Piedmont’s parks and public spaces. The Park Commission will also announce its annual selection of trees for the City’s Heritage Tree program at the event, now in its seventh year. The commission selects heritage trees based on community nominations. Trees in the community are considered for the title based on their aesthetic, educational, or historical significance. Any tree in Piedmont’s parks or public spaces qualifies for consideration. Trees on private land will not be considered. Nominators for selected trees will be recognized at the event. articles.text: Fire Dept. called; traffic stalled during peak hours Morning traffic at the middle and high school faced significant delays shortly after 8 a.m. on Friday, April 19, following a ruptured gas line at the new pool’s construction site. Sometime later, the line was determined to be inactive. Construction crews, as it turns out, had hit an out-of-service gas line on-site near Magnolia Avenue. “When you hit a gas line, typically there is hissing and a very distinctive smell, but that didn’t happen,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. PG&E was called to assess the situation and the fire department was called to close the street until the situation was declared safe. “Typically, during demolition, because PG&E owns the pipeline up until it passes through the meter, they will remove the service meter and cap the gas line at the building, leaving the pipeline in place,” explained Gonzales, “which is what happened here.” Gonzales apologized for the inconvenience to parents and students during their Friday morning drop-off. “Anytime there’s a chance of danger, we want to ensure the greatest safety for our workers and our community,” he said. Sometime later, the line was determined to be inactive. PG&E was called to assess the situation and the fire department was called to close the street until the situation was declared safe. “Typically, during demolition, because PG&E owns the pipeline up until it passes through the meter, they will remove the service meter and cap the gas line at the building, leaving the pipeline in place,” explained Gonzales, “which is what happened here.” Gonzales apologized for the inconvenience to parents and students during their Friday morning drop-off. “Anytime there’s a chance of danger, we want to ensure the greatest safety for our workers and our community,” he said. To be healthy is #2. “Happy” here doesn’t mean ephemeral pleasures, such as a tasty meal, a good cup of coffee, a ‘frivolous’ book, a movie, getting a nice car, gambling, or watching sports. Last pop quiz: If you could only ask one question to figure out if someone will be happy today, what would it be? Okay, a few possibilities popped into your mind this time right? Let’s come back to that and offer the answer. In a Gallup World survey of 1,551,362 adults collected from 164 nations, the largest, most representative sample of the world’s population, the best predictor of the amount of positive emotions felt today was: “Did you learn something new yesterday?” Interesting, right? But, so what? Learning something is meaningful, and meaning is what creates a life of joy, which is truly what parents wish for their children, above all. In exploring how individuals find meaning in life – essentially, how they discover sustained fulfillment and joy – it is apparent that there are four cornerstones central to this pursuit: 1. Discovery: This involves a continual quest for personal understanding and the exploration of one’s desires and capacities. It’s about unraveling the layers of who we are and what we truly seek from life. human experience. Purpose is central to meaning, and after happiness and health, it is the 3rd most wished for by parents. people, places, or things. It is a profound force that drives much of human interaction and fulfillment. 2. Expression: Stemming from the insights gained t h r o u g h self-discovery, expression is the process of showcasing ou r i n ner s elve s t o the world. This can be through art, communication, or any for m that allows one to convey their p e r s o n a l essence. 3. Service: This cornerstone asks, “How can I contribute to the betterment of others?” It is about extending oneself beyond personal needs to aid and uplift others, thereby enriching the communal 4. Love: Representing deep connections and affections, love may be directed towards These cornerstones manifest differently depending on one’s life stage, cultural background, and personal circumstances. For instance, a monk might prioritize service and love, while a young adult m ay fo c u s more intensely on discovery and express i o n . T h e cultural environment also plays a significant role in shaping which c or ne r s t o ne predominates in an individual’s life. The people around us act as branches supporting our life’s tree, providing context and meaning. While not inherently meaningful – similar to being alone in a crowd or having numerous online contacts with few deep connections – the true value in relationships comes through these cornerstones. They help us discover ourselves, express our inner thoughts, commit acts of service, and experience love. The depth of these relationships, much like the thickness of branches, determines their impact on our lives, influencing how we find meaning and joy. However, finding and sustaining this sense of meaning is not without challenges. Fear is a significant hindrance; it stifles our ability to engage with life’s cornerstones by shifting our focus towards immediate safety and comfort. Another less obvious obstacle is the pursuit of fleeting happiness, which can distract from the deeper, more fulfilling joy that comes from engaging with our foundational cornerstones. these four cornerstones, individuals can transcend the ordinary, finding not just happiness but profound joy and fulfillment in their lives. For more resources on creating a meaningful life, visit the nonprofit organization ameaningoflife.org, a comprehensive platform dedicated to helping individuals live more purposefully and joyfully. With summer approaching, parents are starting to plan how to keep their middle school students engaged, focused, and with a certain level of structure when For parents of creative students or students who want to learn art, there is one easy choice: the Young Artist Studio Program (YASP) at California College of the Arts in San Francisco. YASP is a summer art program, where over the course of one week, sixth, seventh, and eighth grade students of all skill levels gain hands-on experience in art-making within a chosen medium from a wide selection of offerings, from animation or graphic design to illustration or fashion design, jewelry making and painting, “Trying to decide what to have your kids do each summer is tricky as it has to fit both the kids’ interest and the parents’ schedule, which sometimes is impossible to align,” said Ryan Parham, associate director of Studio Operations at CCA. “Our approach has been to find those summer camps and activities kids don’t have access to within their typical school year – surf camp, circus camp, and skateboard camp. These YASP weeks fit right in.” Reasons why the program is a favorite among Bay Area students. #1 A wide variety of individual studios to match student interests. Students have many options to explore art making. And with such studio offerings as Animation, Ceramics & Drawing, Illustration & Drawing, Jewelry Making & Metal Arts, and Fashion Design & Illustration, it can be difficult to choose just one. (This summer, YASP offerings have expanded to two sessions: one in June and one in August.) #2 Opportunities to learn something brand new or deepen artistic skills. Although YASP students select just one topic to focus on for the duration of the program, tailored instruction with practicing professionals allows students to try something completely new or build on what they already know. The studios are also praised for their depth and instruction of both the fundamentals and development of artistic techniques. #3 New friendships and a taste of professionalism. The Young Artist Studio Program’s week of activities culminates in a special exhibition of student work on campus. It gives students a preview at professional practices as well as a fun celebration of their achievements. When they reflect on the experience, YASP parents say a favorite for their students is the friends they make and the community they build. “They have a wonderful opportunity to meet and interact with other intro/extrovert kids outside of their typical friend group which has really reduced their fear in meeting new people,” says Ryan Parham, associate director of Studio Operations at CCA.. “They come back each day energized from what they have learned, who they have met, and what they plan to do the next day.” We’ve got summer covered for middle schoolers. articles.text: Members of Piedmont High’s track and field team competed in a pair of events on Saturday, April 20. Seven athletes traveled to the Sacramento Meet of Champions at American River College, and the rest of the varsity team went Montgomery High School in Santa Rosa for the Viking Invitational. The Meet of Champions has runners from across the state and is a good precursor to the North Coast Section Meet of Champions on May 18. “I was really impressed by how calm and collected all of our athletes were,” said coach Pouyan Assadi..”They worked through their pre-race process and were in control while also learning about how to get better.” Meet of Champion results Breah Bell competed in two events in Sacramento. She finished fourth in the long jump with a distance of 16 feet, 7.25 inches, and was 15th in the 100 meter dash with a time of 12.72. “Breah’s inching her way down towards the school record and I’ll admit my heart pounds with excitement every time she gets into the blocks,” Assadi said. She’s been ultra consistent and now has a couple last things to work on for her final leap [in long jump]. She’ll have at least a couple more cracks at it so we’ll see what happens,” Assadi said. Jamie Schwarz finishing 16th of 32 half milers in the 800, clocking a time of 2:24.03. Ella Yasar competed in the 300 meter hurdles with a time of 48.30 seconds. Sebastien Swain continued a strong freshman year, placing ninth of 33 runners in the 800 with a time of 1:58.07. “Seb continues his prolific freshman season. articles.text: The Wildwood Dads Club successfully hosted the second year of its charity golf-tournament on April 19, celebrating another year of fund raising for Wildwood School. A total of 20 dads took Friday off from work to play a round of golf at Oakmoore Golf Course in Stockton, a par-3 course designed for small tournaments. The day started with an 8:00 a.m. pickup at the Community Center. With breakfast burritos in hand the dads enjoyed one another’s company on the one-hour trip to the first tee. “It was a great opportunity to build community with other Piedmont dads while raising muchneeded funds for our schools,” said Havens dad Vipul Kumar. “Reed Johnson and the rest of the Wildwood Dads’ Club did a great job planning. Everyone had a blast.” “It has become the culmination of a year of Dad’s Club events that strengthen the bonds of the community and friendship we all love here in Piedmont,” said Johnson. “The day was filled with sunshine and good times by Wildwood dads and a Havens dad. Hopefully, we can continue to build the Wildwood dad community and also inter-school dads’ club relationships,” said Rohit Giri. Trophies were awarded for longest drive, longest putt, and best golf outfit. Following the golf. they had a barbeque with ribs and hot dogs. articles.text: Although the 3rd Annual Food Fest in Piedmont Park was brimming with a smorgasbord of exciting eats, food wasn’t the only attraction at the event. The Food Fest also served as a celebration of the Bay Area’s diverse culture. “Three years ago, we set out to do something that celebrated the diversity of the Bay,” said founder Roger Tsai to the audience. “Today, we get to do just that.” The day’s entertainment started on a stage in Piedmont Park with a performance by the Great Wall Youth Orchestra, a youth group from Oakland specializing in traditional Chinese music and opera played on authentic Chinese instruments. The Oh Hina’aro Nui Tahitian Dance School from Brisbane gave an exciting display of traditional Tahitian dances by their youth classes, beginner classes, and professional soloists. Oakland Taiko brought an energetic fervor to the stage as the third act of the day. The East Bay community dojo pounded drums with such passion that it brought out residents from houses surrounding the park. “I live nearby and I was pretty tired from my day, but I heard the drums and I had to come out. They just called to me”, joked Celeste Boyd, who lives near the park. In a brief reprieve from the high-energy acts of the morning, professional chef James Yeun Leong Parry took the stage for a Q&A session about what it is like to work in the culinary world. Parry is the creator of Happy Crane, a critically acclaimed Cantonese pop-up restaurant in San Francisco. The Devendra Sharma Folk Ensemble performed a series of Nautanki, a form of North Indian musical theater passed down through oral tradition. After receiving funding for a full-scale production in 2021, the company will be performing their production of Princess Nautanki next month in San Francisco along with musicians from India as well as local singers and dancers from the Bay Area. articles.text: Berkeley Symphony will present a concert titled Pictures at an Exhibition on Sunday, June 2 at 4 p.m. in Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus. The final Symphonic Series concert of the 2023-24 season, led by Music Director Joseph Young, seeks to bring color and light together in a program of mesmerizing symphonic works by Jimmy López Bellido, Duke Ellington, and Modest Mussorgsky. “Throughout our 52nd season, we’ve explored musical colors and styles, welcomed a diversity of artists, and created orchestral experiences that are powerful, joyful, and inclusive,” said Young. “I dedicate this final program to all who went on this musical journey with us, especially the musicians of the Berkeley Symphony and the audiences who turned out to support us all season long.” Leticia Moreno, a Spanish-born violinist, will perform in the West Coast premiere of Jimmy López Bellido’s violin concerto, Aurora, following its successful world premiere performance and GRAMMY-nominated recording with the Houston Symphony. López Bellido’s previous work, Rise, was commissioned by Berkeley Symphony and premiered in 2022. López Bellido said he was inspired to write Aurora after seeing the Northern Lights, which he described as “one of Nature’s most spectacular displays.” The program also includes Duke Ellington’s wistful “Solitude,” a 1934 jazz standard Spanish-born violinist Leticia Moreno will perform with Berkeley Symphony. recorded numerous times by Ellington, that will return to Zellerbach Hall via Morton Gould’s string orchestra arrangement. Ellington famously wrote this brief yet poignant work in only 20 minutes, but the piece has left a lasting legacy in the music world. The program’s final piece, Mussorgsky’s Pictures at an Exhibition, began as a romantic suite for solo piano but was expanded by Maurice Ravel’s magnificent orchestration to depict scenes by Mussorgsky’s contemporary, Russian architect and painter Viktor Hartmann. Audiences are invited to a 3 p.m. pre-concert chat, moderated by Berkeleyside journalist Andrew Gilbert. Tickets for Pictures at an Exhibition start at $25 and can be purchased online at www.berkeleysymphony.org or by calling 841-2800. Music Director Joseph Young will lead the orchestra in Pictures at an Exhibition, the final symphonic series concert of the 2023-2024 season.

articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet has announced its 2024-25 season, which includes modern works by today’s celebrated choreographers and an expansion of the company’s own classical lexicon. Curated and led by Artistic Director Tamara Rojo, this season will feature works by Dutch choreographer Hans van Manen, and contemporary choreographers Christopher Wheeldon, Akram Khan, Wayne McGregor, and Annabelle Lopez Ochoa. The season will begin in December with the holiday favorite Nutcracker, set in San Francisco and honoring the company’s legacy as the first to present a full-length production of the show. “Across an extraordinary 2024 season, I have been deeply inspired by the incredibly talented artists of our world-renowned company and our audiences in San Francisco. In 2025, SF Ballet will explore a range of choreographic and artistic styles and deliver profound human connections through dance—from seduction to heartbreak, and from stories of conflict to gothic science-fiction,” Rojo said. articles.text: South African saxophonist McCoy Mrubata In celebration of South African Freedom Day, SF Jazz welcomes South African saxophonist McCoy Mrubata to the Miner Auditorium stage for two performances this Sunday, April 28. Mrubata hails from Cape Town’s historic Langa township and grew up with the sounds of African music, including the soulful hymns of the Zion Church, the chants and rhythms of traditional healers and the music of the Merry Macs band. In the aftermath of the 1976 uprising, McCoy studied informally under Langa greats including Madoda Gxabeka, Winston Ngozi, the Ngcukanas, Ezra and Duke, Blackie Tempi and Robert Sithole. By the early 1980s, he was playing in cover bands Fever, Touch, Airborne, and Vukani. He gained inter national fame in 1992 when he toured the world with Hugh Masekela’s Lerapo band and has collaborated with Brazilian artists Airto and Flora Purim. Mrubata’s albums have won numerous awards, including the South African Music Award for best traditional jazz release. What were the greatest musical performances of all time? Those were the recordings on the famous program radio program, The Hit Parade. Fortunately, the public had a chance to voice its opinion. But what about the bottom of the list? How about the worst recordings ever made? You guessed it… the debate rages. And along with this debate, there is a lot of misinformation. Many composers have had a chance to tickle the musical funnybone. Mozart knew how to do it, perhaps better than any other composer. He had a lusty sense of humor bordering on the vulgar. Listen to his composition “The Musical Joke” where his bawdy sense of humor is shown to best advantage. Hardly any other composer knew how to parody wayward amateur musicians at their worst. The musicians get lost and wander around trying to find the exit. Somewhere along the way they have musical indigestion, resulting in flatulence. No one can listen to this music without bursting out in laughter. The same can be said for the infamous singer Florence Foster Jenkins. Did she know how terrible she was or was this a ruse to gain publicity? Either way, her fame persists. The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet Other famous singers have made silly recordings. Some of them were great opera singers. Some of them were pop singers, imitating other pop singers. Of these, my favorite is Johnny Cash imitating Elvis Presley. Many people consider Jascha Heifetz to be the greatest violinist of all time. He also had a perfectly timed sense of humor. And herein the debate also rages. He frequently used the initials JH to create a pseudonym. For example he wrote some pop songs using the pseudonym Jim Hoyle. There is also a violinist by the name of Joseph Hague. Once again, the initials JH. Joseph Hague was a terrible violinist. In fact, his inability to play was “perfectly” awful. Some people have made a case that Joseph Hague was a real person. The truth is that Hague was “perfectly” horrible and the violinist was actually Jascha Heifetz making a comedy recording. I know this for a fact. Part of the proof is on YouTube in a video entitled “Jascha Heifetz… The audition.” Heifetz pulled this routine on very rare occasions, and was always a surprise to his students. I remember witnessing one of these events. The playing was awful. In fact, it was perfectly awful. There are other recordings in the same vein played by Jascha Heifetz. The names of the violinists are Victor Belmont and Victor Belmor. All of these violinists are played by the same performer. The names of the piano accompanists are also ridiculous. Floyd E. Sharp for example. Look at the photo on the cover of the record. It is a photo of Jascha Heifetz with an innocuous head glued atop. The violin is Heifetz Guarnerius. He never let anyone touch it. In fact, he never let anyone even look at it for any length of time. I bought one of these records in a Salvation Army store in the 1960s for $.25. It’s worth a lot more now. Heifetz is enjoying a good laugh. pages.text: Wednesday, April 24, 2024 27 Features By Josh Harkinson I dug and planted my first vegetable garden when I was 10. I can’t remember why. My mother says I wanted to sell vegetables on the driveway. The tomatoes – giant beefsteaks that were more than we could eat – ripened around the same time that the neighbor had a garage sale. I put up a table nearby to capitalize on the footfall and sold out much faster than our neighbor did. Years later after starting my own family, I always planted a vegetable garden. My two toddlers quickly learned to appreciate where food came from. They would spend hours each week foraging. A bean teepee built from bamboo poles doubled as a fort. The kids learned to be mindful of fragile stems. Waiting to pick things until they were perfectly ripe taught them patience. Now that I have a preteen and teenager, the vegetable garden continues to play a central role in our lives. The kids help me amend the soil and plant the seedlings. When they get home from school on their razor scooters, they usually pause in the yard to nibble a few raspberries or pick an orange and eat it on the bench overlooking the creek. My daughter has become our resident salad expert, adding spicy and peppery greens from the yard to our store-bought lettuces. Planting vegetables in your yard does not necessarily require turning it into Green Acres. There are advantages to farmlike raised beds with uniform rows of plantings (more on that in a minute), but personally I like to integrate my edibles with my flowering decorative plants. For example, my tomatoes grow in a front-yard bed along the sidewalk, but the street-facing side of it has ceanothus, salvia, and butterfly bush that provide color, attract pollinators, and prevent passersby from swiping the juicy red fruits come August. In the cold season, I replace the tomatoes with winter greens. April and May are the perfect months to plant your summer vegetables. Make sure you give yourself time to prepare. Many root vegetables and certainly tomatoes require very rich, welldrained, loosely tilled soil. To create my tomato patch, I dug down about 18 inches and took out all large rocks. I removed about a third of the soil and added enough manure (for nitrogen), peat moss (for water retention and acidity), and sand (for drainage) to more than replace it. It was hard, sweaty work. Too bad my kids weren’t teenagers back then or else I could have used them as free labor. The ideal soil amendment will depend upon your initial conditions. The more clay you have, the more you will need to amend it. In general, you want the soil to look dark brown and crumbly and to smell like a ripe cow pasture. If you are using raised beds, you won’t need to dig as deep, but you’ll need to add a lot more soil. Don’t forget to run irrigation. Vegetables require more water than most ornamentals. I don’t like soaker hoses because they constantly spring leaks. Consider using a system with adjustable spray nozzles. Your first tomato harvest will be amazing. Your third or fourth, not so much. Tomatoes rapidly suck nutrients from the ground. Later, you can use nitrogen-fixing plants to revive your soil. In my garden, I’ve also had great success with summer squash and cucumbers. Just be aware that these plants can take up a lot of space. One solution is to trellis them. You can even use a bamboo teepee as with pole Photos by Josh Harkinson A massive heirloom tomato from our garden. My daughter with her tomato harvest. A front-yard tomato patch. articles.text: Part 1 wines for a few extra years of aging before release, in fact, one wine Longue Gard (long keeping ) they were pouring a current release from 2014. The classic red cuvee was also outstanding as were the rose and white wines. (VOS Selections) It all started with Jim Harrison. One of my favorite writers, Harrison is the author of the novella Legends of the Fall which was made into a movie with Brad Pitt. He is also author of several collections of books on food and wine that were collected from his years as food columnist for Esquire magazine. Time and again in his essays he would rhapsodize about the wines of Bandol particularly Domaine Tempier. After years of reading about his favorite wine I decided I needed to discover Bandol wines for myself. So along with my colleagues Richard Wing and Terry Hershey after four days exploring the wines of Burgundy, we set off for the four-hour drive south to sunny Bandol. France is world-renowned as a gastronomic center of excellence, yet it has more McDonald’s per capita than any other country. Bandol is world-renowned for its complex age-worthy reds, but 80% of its production is rose. Count it up to the French paradox. The Bandol wine region is just east of Marseilles perched high on limestone cliffs that overlooks the cerulean blue waters of the Mediterranean and the fishing village of Bandol. The seaside resort district is filled with rocky beaches, seafood stands, patio brasseries and palm trees. There is no better place to drink rose – or make it. But our quest was for the mighty reds of Bandol. Crafted from up to 95% Mourvedre grapes, the region is the king of that grape and home to red wines that can compete with the greatest of the Rhone Valley in power and complexity. We settled into a comfortable Air B&B house in the charming seaside town of La Ciotat that we used as our base for four days of exploration. Le Galantin Bandol is one of the great values of the region. FAVORITE WINE • 2014 Le Galantin Bandol Longue Gard Plush with a rich, silky decadence, that reminded me of Chateauneuf du Pape. Plump, succulent ripe plum and blueberry flavors with a huge mouthfeel but plenty of acid and structure to keep it from being flabby. This wine is drinking perfectly at ten years of age but will easily age for another decade. If you cannot find this cuvee the regular cuvee of Galantin Bandol is equally excellent.
articles.title: The wines of Bandol

articles.text: This is the granddaddy of all Bandol wineries. Situated on the outskirts of Saint Cyr-sur-Mer the estate has been in the hands of the Portalis family since before the French Revolution. The estate was devastated during the French Revolution and suffered the effects of the phylloxera epidemic in the 19th century. The estate is currently under the direction of Cyrille Portalis assisted by his wife Magali and his two sons Etienne and Edouard. We were greeted by Etienne and led into the tasting room next to the old house. He gently reminded his American guests that the table we were standing in front of was older than our country. They started with a wine called Bienfait des Pradeaux made from young vines. It was light and fruity and would make a good picnic wine and at 10 euros was a good bargain. Then on to the main show. The red Bandols of Chateaux Pradeaux were some of the biggest most massive and tannic wines we had on our whole trip. They were highly concentrated and build to withstand decades in the cellar which made them slightly challenging to drink at such a young age. Patience however will be rewarded with these Nicola at La Bastide Blanche. The ancient Mourvèdre vines of La Bastide Blanche.
articles.title: Chateaux Pradeaux

articles.text: This estate is run by Alain Pascal and named after his father Honore who was indeed Gros (big). He farms sixteen hectares of vineyards on the hillsides of La Cadiere d’Azur. The vineyards are composed of both clay and limestone, imparting a pronounced structure of earthy splintered rock. This microclimate near the Mediterranean brings warm weather and full sun tempered by the Mistral winds. His red wines use 80% Mourvedre for additional strength and boldness. They make a charming rose along with the mainstay red wines. They have vintages for sale going back to 2005. (Kermit Lynch Imports) Gros Nore available at Kermit Lynch Wines. FAVORITE WINE • 2015 Gros Nore Bandol Cuvee IX This is 90% Mourvedre. It is medium to full-bodied, concentrated and supple, framed by tannins that grow in intensity on the long finish, culminating in a potent but ripe savoriness. It’s a great effort that should age two decades or more.
articles.title: Domaine Gros Nore

articles.text: This has been one of my favorite Bandols. The estate is located in the foothills of SainteBrune Mountain near the Mediterranean. The major grape is Mourvedre of course with additional plantings of Grenache, Cinsault and Clairette. We were greeted by Nicola son of the founders who grew up on the estate and now teaches law nearby. He began the tasting with the 2022 Cuvee Estagnol Blanc a blend of Clairette and Ugni Blanc intensely flavored of apricots and peaches with a huge mouthfeel. One of the best white wines of the entire trip. The 2022 Rose got the nod over the 2023. The regular cuvee red wine from 2020 was Pascale hosting us at Gros Nore.
articles.title: La Bastide Blanche

articles.text: This is one of the wineries I was most excited to visit as it is easily available in the US and is often the most affordable Bandol in the market. Founded in 1960 with the first production in 1972, it is a family operation now run by Celine Pascale and her brother Jerome with mother and father still helping. pages.text: 28 Wednesday, April 24, 2024 The Wine Corner The wines of Bandol Part 1 wines for a few extra years of aging before release, in fact, one wine Longue Gard (long keeping ) they were pouring a current release from 2014. The classic red cuvee was also outstanding as were the rose and white wines. (VOS Selections) By Pierre DuMont It all started with Jim Harrison. One of my favorite writers, Harrison is the author of the novella Legends of the Fall which was made into a movie with Brad Pitt. He is also author of several collections of books on food and wine that were collected from his years as food columnist for Esquire magazine. Time and again in his essays he would rhapsodize about the wines of Bandol particularly Domaine Tempier. After years of reading about his favorite wine I decided I needed to discover Bandol wines for myself. So along with my colleagues Richard Wing and Terry Hershey after four days exploring the wines of Burgundy, we set off for the four-hour drive south to sunny Bandol. France is world-renowned as a gastronomic center of excellence, yet it has more McDonald’s per capita than any other country. Bandol is world-renowned for its complex age-worthy reds, but 80% of its production is rose. Count it up to the French paradox. The Bandol wine region is just east of Marseilles perched high on limestone cliffs that overlooks the cerulean blue waters of the Mediterranean and the fishing village of Bandol. The seaside resort district is filled with rocky beaches, seafood stands, patio brasseries and palm trees. There is no better place to drink rose – or make it. But our quest was for the mighty reds of Bandol. Crafted from up to 95% Mourvedre grapes, the region is the king of that grape and home to red wines that can compete with the greatest of the Rhone Valley in power and complexity. We settled into a comfortable Air B&B house in the charming seaside town of La Ciotat that we used as our base for four days of exploration. Domaine le Galantin This is one of the wineries I was most excited to visit as it is easily available in the US and is often the most affordable Bandol in the market. Founded in 1960 with the first production in 1972, it is a family operation now run by Celine Pascale and her brother Jerome with mother and father still helping. Galantin keeps their Le Galantin Bandol is one of the great values of the region. FAVORITE WINE • 2014 Le Galantin Bandol Longue Gard Plush with a rich, silky decadence, that reminded me of Chateauneuf du Pape. Plump, succulent ripe plum and blueberry flavors with a huge mouthfeel but plenty of acid and structure to keep it from being flabby. This wine is drinking perfectly at ten years of age but will easily age for another decade. If you cannot find this cuvee the regular cuvee of Galantin Bandol is equally excellent. La Bastide Blanche This has been one of my favorite Bandols. The estate is located in the foothills of SainteBrune Mountain near the Mediterranean. The major grape is Mourvedre of course with additional plantings of Grenache, Cinsault and Clairette. We were greeted by Nicola son of the founders who grew up on the estate and now teaches law nearby. He began the tasting with the 2022 Cuvee Estagnol Blanc a blend of Clairette and Ugni Blanc intensely flavored of apricots and peaches with a huge mouthfeel. One of the best white wines of the entire trip. The 2022 Rose got the nod over the 2023. The regular cuvee red wine from 2020 was Celine Pascale of Le Galantin. Pascale hosting us at Gros Nore. Tasting with Etienne at Chateaux Pradeaux. outstanding and a great value. For historical purposes they poured a 2007 Red Bandol which was in immaculate shape and a 1999 whose fruit had faded just slightly but still pleased with an ethereal perfumed nose. Weygandt-Metzler Imports) FAVORITE WINE • 2016 Bastide Blanche Bandol Cuvee Estagnol This bottling just edged out its sister wine Cuvee Fontaneou as champ. It is 98% Mourvedre and is inky black showing seductive scents of vanilla, cedar, blackberries, plums, and earth. Full-bodied and rich on the palate with great structure and layers of flavor on the long finish. Domaine Gros Nore This estate is run by Alain Pascal and named after his father Honore who was indeed Gros (big). He farms sixteen hectares of vineyards on the hillsides of La Cadiere d’Azur. The vineyards are composed of both clay and limestone, imparting a pronounced structure of earthy splintered rock. This microclimate near the Mediterranean brings warm weather and full sun tempered by the Mistral winds. His red wines use 80% Mourvedre for additional strength and boldness. They make a charming rose along with the mainstay red wines. They have vintages for sale going back to 2005. (Kermit Lynch Imports) Chateaux Pradeaux This is the granddaddy of all Bandol wineries. Situated on the outskirts of Saint Cyr-sur-Mer the estate has been in the hands of the Portalis family since before the French Revolution. The estate was devastated during the French Revolution and suffered the effects of the phylloxera epidemic in the 19th century. The estate is currently under the direction of Cyrille Portalis assisted by his wife Magali and his two sons Etienne and Edouard. We were greeted by Etienne and led into the tasting room next to the old house. He gently reminded his American guests that the table we were standing in front of was older than our country. They started with a wine called Bienfait des Pradeaux made from young vines. It was light and fruity and would make a good picnic wine and at 10 euros was a good bargain. Then on to the main show. The red Bandols of Chateaux Pradeaux were some of the biggest most massive and tannic wines we had on our whole trip. They were highly concentrated and build to withstand decades in the cellar which made them slightly challenging to drink at such a young age. Patience however will be rewarded with these wines as they are sure to grown in complexity and refinement as they age. (Neal Rosenthal Imports) Massive and full-bodied Pradeaux red Bandol. FAVORITE WINE • 2019 Chateaux Pradeaux Bandol Made from 95% Mourvedre and 5% Cinsault the wine showed a brooding nose of violets, cassis and blackberries. In the mouth it was massive and full with tons of dark berry fruit, leather, earth and stone. It was layered and complex with a long, tannin-filled finish. Put this in the cellar and forget it for a decade. Nicola at La Bastide Blanche. Gros Nore available at Kermit Lynch Wines. FAVORITE WINE • 2015 Gros Nore Bandol Cuvee IX This is 90% Mourvedre. It is medium to full-bodied, concentrated and supple, framed by tannins that grow in intensity on the long finish, culminating in a potent but ripe savoriness. It’s a great effort that should age two decades or more. The ancient Mourvèdre vines of La Bastide Blanche.

articles.text: Alma Lowell Dittmer, a professor and writer who worked at UC Berkeley for 40 years and specialized in Chinese politics, died at age 82 on April 15 in Oakland. He was named after his father Alma, but throughout his life went by his middle name, Lowell. His parents Alma and Veda met when they were teachers at a junior high school in Utah. They would spend much of their life teaching; Alma as a university professor of music; his wife as a K-12 teacher with specialties in Home Economics and Remedial Reading. Lowell was the eldest of their six children, and they instilled in him the sense that he ought to be an example for his younger siblings. He went on his Mormon mission to German-speaking Switzerland, an experience that he would credit as being one of the most challenging of his life. He would later speak of being proud of having completed his mission; however, when he returned to Utah, he found he had lost his faith in God, and would describe himself throughout the rest of his life as an atheist or agnostic. He sought out his next challenge in academia, where, after a brief flirtation with journalism, he dove into the field of political science, earning his bachelor’s degree from Utah State in 1965. He then moved to Chicago, where he would begin his career of more than 50 years as a China scholar. He learned to speak Chinese; went to basic training with the U.S. Army reserves; and met Helen Roth, the woman he would marry. He earned his master’s degree in 1967 and his PhD in 1971. His dissertation was published as his first book in 1974: Liu Shao-Ch’i and the Chinese Cultural Revolution. He and Helen were married on August 14 of that year. In 1978, he came to UC Berkeley, where he would become a leading scholar in his field. He wrote, edited, or co-edited over Lowell Dittmer, a University of California professor of Chinese politics, died on April 15, 2024. He was 82. 16 books, as well as probably over 100 articles in scholarly journals. In addition to writing, he also took on interesting responsibilities near and far. He was the head of the UC Center for Chinese Studies from 1979-1983; and then editor-inchief of the Asian Survey from 2001-2019. He was a research fellow at the Smithsonian Institute in Washington, D.C. from 1986- 1987, and later a director for the UC’s Education Abroad Program in Beijing from 1997-1999. His love of work-related travel would never leave him; in the last decade of his life he spent semesters abroad in Singapore, Malaysia, Korea, and Taiwan. He also enjoyed traveling on family trips. He often visited with his wife’s family in Chicago, and to various spots in the U.S. for semi-annual Dittmer family reunions. In his spare time he enjoyed exercise, healthy eating, bargain hunting, listening to music of all kinds, collecting odds and ends (‘one man’s trash is another man’s treasure’), and consuming art and literature – especially foreign-language movies. He is survived by his sisters Ruth Ellen, Kaye, and Debbie; his brothers Kent and Phil; his son Mark, and his wife Helen. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 Hours: Tuesday-Saturday: 11 a.m. – 5:30 p.m. Sunday: 1 p.m – 5 p.m. Donations accepted at 2501 Harrison Street Tuesday & Wednesday: 9 a.m. – 12:00 p.m. Saturdays: 10 a.m. – 12:00 p.m.

To celebrate, they had a special tour of historic Mountain View Cemetery. It was a lovely spring morning and there was a strong turnout of 50 walkers. Dennis first pointed out his “three girlfriends” in front of the “main mausoleum” that was built in 1928. They are statues of ancient Greek women that represent life, and how well and long it is lived. Dennis noted one is holding cissors. The group was led up a hill to the mausoleum of David Douty Colton. He was an associate of the “Big Four” railroad men who bankrolled the construction of the transcontinental railroad and became very wealthy. Dennis said “Big Five” might be a more accurate name. Colton’s mausoleum is a classical revival building with Corinthian columns and an Egyptian sphinx in front. A statue depiction of a cloth was also noted. It represents a pall that covers a casket. Depending on the deceased’s wealth, it could be buried with the person, or just Sketch of Dick Carter by Phil Witte. rented, leading to the term “pallbearers.” Dennis pointed to the many obelisks around the cemetery. They mark graves from the late 19th Century at the time when the Washington Monument was built – a time when the cemetery was being created, and Egyptian archeological discoveries were being made by the western world. Everything Egyptian was the rage. There is a large pyramid built for William Gwin, California’s first senator, and his family. Up the hill is a tall statue of an elk on a monument, marking the section of the cemetery for Elks Club members. The story of renowned landscape architect Fredrick Law Olmsted, who designed the cemetery in 1863 and also designed New York’s Central Park, as well as much of the UC Berkeley and Stanford University campuses. Olmsted was managing gold mines in Bear Valley, California, when he was asked to design the cemetery. There were 197 acres to work with, and 23 more were bought later – now totaling 220 acres. Dennis said the number of people buried in the cemetery is unknown because in the past some people were buried in unendowed areas and not recorded. He estimated there are about 180,000 graves. The group made their up the cemetery’s south boundary and saw Moraga Avenue homes with backyards facing the cemetery. This was the area of Walter Blair’s late 19th and early 20th Century “Blair Park” attraction. Workers were cutting down huge eucalyptus trees. Dennis said the trees were a fall danger and needed to be removed. Further on was a small lake that provides water for the cemetery. Turkeys, deer, fish, and other wildlife also make use of it. Next stop was a small, worn obelisk with a plaque that reads, “Jane Waer 1822–1865 1st Burial in Mountain View Cemetery.” The last stop was the family plot of George Pardee, mayor of Oakland from 1893 to 1895 and California governor from 1903 to 1907. The walkers thanked Dennis Evanosky for a most enjoyable, information-packed tour of a beautiful place on a beautiful morning with a wonderful storyteller. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.
